Forward Control Mopar: Rare 1966 Dodge A100 5-Window Pickup Needs a Home
16 photos
Photo: Craiglist
Dodge's current lineup includes only three vehicles: the Charger coupe, the Charger four-door , and the Durango SUV. But there was a time when Dodge had a more diverse lineup. Moreover, Dodge used to be a big player in the van market.
The Chrysler division actually started the minivan craze in the United States by introducing the Caravan in 1984. It remained in production through 2020. But Dodge also offered full-size vans over the years. The B-Series, also known as the Ram Van, was built from 1971 all the way until 2003.
The Ram Van was replaced by the Sprinter, essentially a rebadged Mercedes-Benz (courtesy of the Daimler-Chrysler merger that lasted until 2007). The Dodge Sprinter was phased out in 2009 as the division's last full-size van. But Dodge's venture in the van market began in 1964 with a compact hauler, the A100.
A replacement for the Town Panel , a panel truck variant of the Dodge C-Series pickup, the A100 was developed to compete with the Ford Econoline and Chevrolet Greenbrier. Both had arrived in 1961 to take on the popular Volkswagen Bus (Type 2). Upon the A100's arrival, Chevrolet replaced the Corvair-based Greenbrier with a new front-engine van.
The A100 was based on the Chrysler A platform, which underpinned Mopar's early compact cars, including the Plymouth Valiant, Plymouth Barracuda, and Dodge Dart. Dodge offered two wheelbases, including a 90-inch variant that was exclusive to the van series.
Much like its Ford and Chevrolet competitors, the A100 came in three versions: a passenger van, a cargo van, and a pickup. The latter is the rarest of the bunch, and the five-window example you see here is even scarcer. The optional five-window treatment added curved rear quarter windows to create a panoramic view.
Dodge did not keep production records based on body styles, but these pickups are hard to come by today. And that's mainly because pickups have a very low survival rate; most rusted away in junkyards and barns over the years.
This two-tone, green-and-white truck that surfaced in Babylon, New York, is in fantastic condition for a 60-year-old A100. It's far from perfect, and the buyer will need to address minor rust issues and cracks in the paint, but this pickup is ready to haul, as it "runs and drives great," according to the seller. And it still relies on the original drivetrain.
Produced through 1970, the A100 was available with four different engines. The lineup included a pair of slant-six units , as well as a pair of V8 powerplants. When it came to the economical inline-six mills, buyers could choose between the 170- and 225-cubic-inch (2.8- and 3.7-liter) displacements.
On the V8 front, offerings included two small-block powerplants displacing 273 and 318 cubic inches (4.5 and 5.2 liters). The latter was the most potent at 210 horsepower. This A100 was ordered with the optional 225 inline-six, which came with 145 horsepower on tap. It's paired with a three-speed manual transmission.
The seller wants $11,500 to let this pickup go. For reference, project units fetch below $10K, while driver-quality examples can cost over $17,000. Some restored examples have sold for over $25,000 in recent years.
Fun fact: Some of Chrysler's factory-built Super Stock cars were equipped with A100 front seats to save weight. The list includes the 1965 Dodge Coronet A990 and Plymouth Belvedere A990, as well as the 1968 Dodge Dart L023 and Plymouth Barracuda B029 (both with Hemi engines).

Image: PlugShare
PlugShare is giving its EV charging app a big overhaul. Version 8.0 arrives worldwide for iPhone on November 10, with dark mode, a trip planner that shows how far apart charging stops are, and a rebuilt Apple Watch app that can point you to a charger compatible with your EV.
What’s new in PlugShare 8.0
Dark mode was one of the most-requested features from PlugShare users. It works across the app and follows your iPhone’s settings, so if your phone switches to dark mode at sunset, your charging map will, too.
The trip planner gets a small but handy change. Each charging stop now shows how far it is from both the start of your trip and the previous stop. So when you’re deciding whether to stretch to the next fast charger or stop sooner, the number you need is right there.
PlugShare now loads your saved locations, trips, and profile when you open the app or sign in, so those tabs are ready to tap. You can also open and zoom in on station photos right from their thumbnails. That’s handy when you’re trying to figure out what corner a charging station is in in a big parking lot. The app also adapts its layout to the iPhone Duo’s different screens and folded positions.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Find a charger from your Apple Watch
The rebuilt Watch app lists nearby charging stations with distances and directions. It uses the filters you’ve set on your iPhone, so if you’ve filtered for plugs that fit your EV, that carries over to your wrist.
Tap a station and you’ll see its PlugScore, the network that runs it, a small map, and which plugs it has, including NACS, CCS, CHAdeMO, or J1772. The list refreshes when you raise your wrist and open the app. You can also add a shortcut to a round or corner slot on your watch face.
The iPhone update is rolling out through the App Store . PlugShare says Android users will get dark mode and a redesign based on Google’s Material 3 in early 2027.
